CHAPTER 3 - TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS-I

Introduction

Trigonometry began as the study of triangles, but it grows into one of the most powerful tools in all of mathematics. In this chapter we free the trigonometric ratios from the right triangle and turn them into FUNCTIONS defined for ANY angle - positive or negative, small or large. We first learn how angles are measured in degrees and in radians, then define the six trigonometric functions of a general angle, study their signs in the four quadrants, evaluate them at the standard angles, prove the fundamental identities, and finally examine their domain, range, periodicity and graphs. These ideas are the foundation for everything that follows: solving equations, modelling waves and oscillations, and the calculus of periodic phenomena.

3.1 ANGLES AND THEIR MEASUREMENT

An ANGLE is formed when a ray rotates about its end point (the vertex) from an initial position (the initial side) to a final position (the terminal side). If the rotation is anticlockwise the angle is taken as POSITIVE; if clockwise it is NEGATIVE. This sense of rotation lets angles be as large as we like and also negative - a great advance over the schoolbook angle that lies between 0 and 90 degrees.

There are two common units for measuring angles.

DEGREE MEASURE. One complete revolution is divided into 360 equal parts; each part is one degree (1 degree). One degree is divided into 60 minutes (60') and one minute into 60 seconds (60''). Thus a right angle is 90 degrees and a straight angle is 180 degrees.

RADIAN MEASURE. A more natural unit for higher mathematics is the radian. One RADIAN is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius of the circle. Since the full circumference of a circle of radius r is 2*pi*r, a complete revolution subtends an angle of (2*pi*r)/r = 2*pi radians. Therefore

   2*pi radians = 360 degrees,   so   pi radians = 180 degrees.

This is the key relation connecting the two systems. From it,

   1 radian = 180/pi degrees = about 57 degrees 16 minutes,
   1 degree = pi/180 radians = about 0.01745 radian.

To convert a degree measure to radians, multiply by pi/180; to convert a radian measure to degrees, multiply by 180/pi. For example, 30 degrees = 30 * pi/180 = pi/6 radian, and 45 degrees = pi/4 radian, and 60 degrees = pi/3 radian, and 90 degrees = pi/2 radian.

ARC LENGTH. If an arc of length s of a circle of radius r subtends an angle theta (measured IN RADIANS) at the centre, then

   theta = s / r,   so   s = r * theta.

This simple formula only works when theta is in radians - one of the main reasons radian measure is preferred. The area of the corresponding sector is A = (1/2) r^2 theta.

Worked example. A wheel of radius 20 cm turns through an angle of 3 radians. The point on the rim moves through an arc length s = r*theta = 20 * 3 = 60 cm.

Worked example. Convert 210 degrees to radians. 210 * pi/180 = 7*pi/6 radian.

3.2 TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS OF ANY ANGLE

To define the trigonometric functions of a general angle we use a coordinate system. Place the vertex of the angle at the origin O and its initial side along the positive x-axis. Let the terminal side, after a rotation of angle theta, pass through a point P(x, y) at a distance r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) from the origin (r is always positive). The six trigonometric functions are defined as ratios of x, y and r:

   sin theta = y / r          cosec theta = r / y
   cos theta = x / r          sec theta   = r / x
   tan theta = y / x          cot theta   = x / y

From these definitions the reciprocal relations follow at once:

   cosec theta = 1 / sin theta,   sec theta = 1 / cos theta,   cot theta = 1 / tan theta,

and also   tan theta = sin theta / cos theta   and   cot theta = cos theta / sin theta.

Because x and y can be positive, negative or zero, these definitions make sense for ANY angle, not just an acute one. When P lies in the first quadrant and theta is acute, x, y and r are all positive and the ratios reduce to the familiar right-triangle ratios (opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse, opposite/adjacent). But now we can also speak of sin 200 degrees or cos(-40 degrees).

Note that tan theta and sec theta are undefined when x = 0 (that is at theta = 90 degrees, 270 degrees, ...), and cot theta and cosec theta are undefined when y = 0 (at theta = 0, 180 degrees, ...), because we cannot divide by zero.

3.3 SIGNS OF THE FUNCTIONS IN THE FOUR QUADRANTS

The sign of each trigonometric function depends on the signs of x and y, which change from quadrant to quadrant (r is always positive):

 - First quadrant (0 to 90 degrees): x > 0, y > 0. ALL six functions are positive.
 - Second quadrant (90 to 180 degrees): x < 0, y > 0. Only SINE (and its reciprocal cosec) is positive.
 - Third quadrant (180 to 270 degrees): x < 0, y < 0. Only TANGENT (and cot) is positive.
 - Fourth quadrant (270 to 360 degrees): x > 0, y < 0. Only COSINE (and sec) is positive.

A popular memory aid is ASTC - "All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine" - read anticlockwise from the first quadrant. A common mnemonic is "All Students Take Calculus." This tells you which function is positive in each quadrant.

ALLIED ANGLES. Angles associated with a given angle theta by adding or subtracting multiples of 90 degrees (or pi/2) are called ALLIED angles - for example (90 - theta), (90 + theta), (180 - theta), (180 + theta), (270 - theta), (270 + theta), (360 - theta), and -theta. Their trigonometric functions can always be reduced to functions of theta by two rules:
 (1) If the angle is (180 +/- theta) or (360 +/- theta) - that is an even multiple of 90 degrees plus/minus theta - the function NAME stays the same (sin stays sin, cos stays cos).
 (2) If the angle is (90 +/- theta) or (270 +/- theta) - an odd multiple of 90 degrees plus/minus theta - the function name CHANGES to its co-function (sin <-> cos, tan <-> cot, sec <-> cosec).
The SIGN of the result is fixed by the ASTC rule applied to the quadrant in which the allied angle lies. For example: sin(180 - theta) = sin theta, cos(180 - theta) = -cos theta, sin(90 + theta) = cos theta, cos(90 + theta) = -sin theta, tan(180 + theta) = tan theta.

3.4 TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS OF STANDARD ANGLES

Certain angles occur so often that their values must be memorised. The values of sine and cosine for the standard angles are:

   angle:   0        30       45       60       90
   sin:     0        1/2      1/sqrt2  sqrt3/2  1
   cos:     1        sqrt3/2  1/sqrt2  1/2      0

A neat pattern helps: write 0,1,2,3,4 under the angles 0,30,45,60,90; divide each by 4, and take the square root - this gives sin. For cos, read the same list backwards. From sine and cosine every other function follows: tan = sin/cos, so

   tan 0 = 0,  tan 30 = 1/sqrt3,  tan 45 = 1,  tan 60 = sqrt3,  tan 90 is undefined.

Worked example. Evaluate sin 30 * cos 60 + cos 30 * sin 60. Using the table this is (1/2)(1/2) + (sqrt3/2)(sqrt3/2) = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1. (In fact this equals sin(30 + 60) = sin 90 = 1.)

Using allied-angle rules the standard values extend to larger angles. For instance sin 120 = sin(180 - 60) = sin 60 = sqrt3/2, cos 135 = cos(180 - 45) = -cos 45 = -1/sqrt2, tan 210 = tan(180 + 30) = tan 30 = 1/sqrt3, sin 150 = sin(180 - 30) = 1/2.

3.5 TRIGONOMETRIC IDENTITIES

An IDENTITY is an equation that is true for every value of the variable for which both sides are defined. The fundamental (Pythagorean) identities come straight from x^2 + y^2 = r^2. Dividing by r^2, x^2 and y^2 in turn gives the three basic identities:

   sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1
   1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta
   1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta

From the first, sin^2 theta = 1 - cos^2 theta and cos^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta. These identities let us find all the ratios once one of them (and the quadrant) is known.

Worked example. If sin theta = 3/5 and theta is in the second quadrant, find cos theta and tan theta. From sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, cos^2 theta = 1 - 9/25 = 16/25, so cos theta = +/- 4/5. In the second quadrant cosine is negative, so cos theta = -4/5, and tan theta = sin/cos = (3/5)/(-4/5) = -3/4.

Together with the reciprocal and quotient relations (cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan, tan = sin/cos), these identities are the workhorses for simplifying expressions and proving further results. For example, (1 - cos^2 theta)/(sin theta) = sin^2 theta / sin theta = sin theta.

3.6 DOMAIN, RANGE, PERIODICITY AND GRAPHS

A function f is PERIODIC with period p if f(theta + p) = f(theta) for every theta, and p is the smallest such positive number. Because a rotation of 360 degrees (2*pi) brings the terminal side back to itself, sine, cosine, cosec and sec repeat every 2*pi, while tangent and cotangent repeat every pi:

   sin(theta + 2*pi) = sin theta,   cos(theta + 2*pi) = cos theta,   tan(theta + pi) = tan theta.

DOMAIN AND RANGE.
 - sin theta and cos theta are defined for ALL real theta; their range is the closed interval [-1, 1].
 - tan theta and sec theta are undefined where cos theta = 0, i.e. at theta = (2n+1)*pi/2. The range of tan is all real numbers; the range of sec is (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity).
 - cot theta and cosec theta are undefined where sin theta = 0, i.e. at theta = n*pi. The range of cot is all real numbers; the range of cosec is (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity).

GRAPHS OF SINE AND COSINE. The graph of y = sin theta is a smooth continuous wave. Starting at the origin (sin 0 = 0) it rises to a maximum of +1 at theta = 90 degrees (pi/2), returns to 0 at 180 degrees (pi), falls to a minimum of -1 at 270 degrees (3*pi/2), and returns to 0 at 360 degrees (2*pi), after which the whole pattern repeats. The graph of y = cos theta has exactly the same wave shape but is shifted: it starts at its maximum +1 at theta = 0, falls to 0 at 90 degrees, to -1 at 180 degrees, back to 0 at 270 degrees and up to +1 at 360 degrees. Thus the cosine curve is the sine curve shifted LEFT by 90 degrees; indeed cos theta = sin(theta + 90 degrees) and sin theta = cos(theta - 90 degrees). Both curves oscillate between -1 and +1 with period 2*pi.

TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS OF NEGATIVE ANGLES. Replacing theta by -theta reflects the point P(x, y) to P'(x, -y), so x is unchanged while y changes sign. Hence

   sin(-theta) = -sin theta   (ODD function)
   cos(-theta) =  cos theta   (EVEN function)
   tan(-theta) = -tan theta   (ODD function)

and likewise cosec(-theta) = -cosec theta, sec(-theta) = sec theta, cot(-theta) = -cot theta. So cosine and secant are even functions (their graphs are symmetric about the y-axis), while the other four are odd functions (their graphs have point symmetry about the origin). For example, sin(-30 degrees) = -sin 30 = -1/2 and cos(-30 degrees) = cos 30 = sqrt3/2.

SUMMARY

- Angles are measured in degrees or radians; one radian is the angle subtended by an arc equal to the radius, and pi radians = 180 degrees. Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by pi/180, radians to degrees by multiplying by 180/pi.
- For an arc of length s subtending angle theta (in radians) at the centre of a circle of radius r, s = r*theta and sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta.
- With the vertex at the origin and P(x, y) on the terminal side at distance r, sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x, and the reciprocals cosec, sec, cot; this defines the functions for ANY angle.
- Signs by quadrant follow ASTC (All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine positive in quadrants I, II, III, IV). Allied-angle formulae reduce functions of 90/180/270/360 +/- theta to functions of theta: the name changes for odd multiples of 90 degrees, stays for even multiples, and the sign comes from ASTC.
- Standard values: sin/cos of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 are 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1 (and reversed for cos); tan of these is 0, 1/sqrt3, 1, sqrt3, undefined.
- Pythagorean identities: sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, 1 + tan^2 = sec^2, 1 + cot^2 = cosec^2, together with the reciprocal and quotient relations.
- sin and cos have domain all reals and range [-1, 1]; tan and cot have range all reals; sec and cosec have range |value| >= 1. Sine, cosine, sec, cosec have period 2*pi; tan and cot have period pi.
- The sine and cosine graphs are identical waves oscillating between -1 and +1, cosine leading sine by 90 degrees.
- Negative angles: sine, tan, cot, cosec are ODD (f(-theta) = -f(theta)); cosine and sec are EVEN (f(-theta) = f(theta)).

topics.name: Measurement of Angles (Degree and Radian)
topics.description: Positive and negative angles by sense of rotation; degree measure (degrees, minutes, seconds) and radian measure; the relation pi radians = 180 degrees; converting between the two systems; arc length s = r*theta and sector area (1/2) r^2 theta with theta in radians.

topics.name: Trigonometric Functions of Any Angle
topics.description: Defining the six functions sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot of a general angle using a point P(x, y) on the terminal side with r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2); reciprocal and quotient relations; where each function is undefined.

topics.name: Signs in Quadrants and Allied Angles
topics.description: Signs of the trigonometric functions in the four quadrants via the ASTC rule (All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine); allied angles (90 +/- theta, 180 +/- theta, 270 +/- theta, 360 +/- theta, -theta) and the name-change / sign rules used to reduce them to functions of theta.

topics.name: Trigonometric Functions of Standard Angles
topics.description: Values of sin, cos and tan at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees; the memory pattern for the table; extending these to larger angles such as 120, 135, 150, 210 degrees using allied-angle relations.

topics.name: Trigonometric Identities
topics.description: The Pythagorean identities sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, 1 + tan^2 = sec^2, 1 + cot^2 = cosec^2, their derivation from x^2 + y^2 = r^2, and their use with the reciprocal/quotient relations to find ratios and simplify expressions.

topics.name: Domain, Range, Periodicity and Graphs
topics.description: Domain and range of the six functions; periodicity (2*pi for sin, cos, sec, cosec; pi for tan, cot); the graphs of sine and cosine described as waves between -1 and +1; even/odd behaviour and trigonometric functions of negative angles.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain positive and negative angles, define degree and radian measure, and state and use the relation pi radians = 180 degrees to convert between degrees and radians.
Apply the arc-length relation s = r*theta (theta in radians) and the sector-area formula (1/2) r^2 theta to solve problems involving arcs, radii and angles.
Define the six trigonometric functions of any angle using a point P(x, y) on the terminal side, and state the reciprocal and quotient relations among them.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Signs in Quadrants and Allied Angles
learning_outcomes.description: Determine the sign of each trigonometric function in the four quadrants using the ASTC rule and reduce allied angles to functions of theta.
Recall and use the values of sin, cos and tan of 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, and evaluate functions of related angles using allied-angle relations.
Derive and apply the Pythagorean identities sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, 1 + tan^2 = sec^2 and 1 + cot^2 = cosec^2 to find ratios and simplify or prove trigonometric expressions.
State the domain, range and period of each trigonometric function and describe the graphs of the sine and cosine functions as waves between -1 and +1.
Analyse the even/odd behaviour of the trigonometric functions and evaluate functions of negative angles using sin(-theta) = -sin theta and cos(-theta) = cos theta.

chapter_summary.title: Trigonometric Functions-I - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics (311) summary develops trigonometry beyond the right triangle. It covers degree and radian measure, the definition of the six functions for any angle, their signs by quadrant and allied angles, values at standard angles, the Pythagorean identities, and the domain, range, periodicity and graphs of the functions.

bullets: Anticlockwise rotation gives a positive angle, clockwise a negative angle; angles can exceed 360 degrees.
One radian is the angle an arc equal in length to the radius subtends at the centre; pi radians = 180 degrees.
Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by pi/180 and radians to degrees by multiplying by 180/pi.
For theta in radians, arc length s = r*theta and sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta.

sections.heading: Functions of any angle
bullets: Put the vertex at the origin and the initial side on the positive x-axis; let P(x, y) lie on the terminal side with r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x, and cosec, sec, cot are their reciprocals.
tan theta = sin theta / cos theta and cot theta = cos theta / sin theta.
tan and sec are undefined when x = 0; cot and cosec are undefined when y = 0.

sections.heading: Signs and allied angles
bullets: ASTC: All positive in quadrant I, only Sine in II, only Tangent in III, only Cosine in IV.
For allied angles the function name stays the same for even multiples of 90 degrees and changes to the co-function for odd multiples.
The sign of the reduced result is fixed by the ASTC rule for the quadrant of the allied angle.
Examples: sin(180 - theta) = sin theta, cos(90 + theta) = -sin theta, tan(180 + theta) = tan theta.

sections.heading: Standard angles and identities
bullets: sin of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 = 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1; cos is the same list reversed.
tan 0 = 0, tan 30 = 1/sqrt3, tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt3, tan 90 is undefined.
Pythagorean identities: sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, 1 + tan^2 = sec^2, 1 + cot^2 = cosec^2.
One known ratio plus the quadrant fixes all the others, e.g. sin = 3/5 in quadrant II gives cos = -4/5, tan = -3/4.

sections.heading: Domain, range, periodicity and graphs
bullets: sin and cos are defined for all real theta with range [-1, 1]; tan and cot have range all reals; sec and cosec have |value| >= 1.
sin, cos, sec, cosec have period 2*pi; tan and cot have period pi.
The sine and cosine graphs are identical waves between -1 and +1, with cosine leading sine by 90 degrees.
sin(-theta) = -sin theta (odd), cos(-theta) = cos theta (even); tan, cot, cosec are odd and sec is even.

key_takeaways: pi radians = 180 degrees; multiply by pi/180 to go from degrees to radians and by 180/pi to go back.
For theta in radians, arc length is s = r*theta and sector area is (1/2) r^2 theta.
Using P(x, y) with r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2): sin = y/r, cos = x/r, tan = y/x, with cosec, sec, cot as reciprocals.
ASTC gives the signs: All in I, Sine in II, Tangent in III, Cosine in IV; allied-angle rules reduce related angles to theta.
Standard values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt2, sin 60 = sqrt3/2; tan 30 = 1/sqrt3, tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt3.
Pythagorean identities: sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, 1 + tan^2 = sec^2, 1 + cot^2 = cosec^2.
sin and cos have period 2*pi and range [-1, 1]; sine is an odd function and cosine is an even function.

glossary.definition: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius; 2*pi radians make one full revolution and pi radians = 180 degrees.
A unit of angle equal to 1/360 of a full revolution, subdivided into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds.
The starting ray (initial side, along the positive x-axis) and the final ray (terminal side) of an angle after rotation about the vertex.
An angle measured anticlockwise is positive; one measured clockwise is negative.
s = r*theta, the length of a circular arc of radius r subtending angle theta (in radians) at the centre.
The area of a circular sector, (1/2) r^2 theta, with theta measured in radians.
sin, cos, tan and their reciprocals defined from a point P(x, y) on the terminal side as ratios of x, y and r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
A memory aid (All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine) giving which functions are positive in quadrants I, II, III and IV respectively.
Angles of the form 90 +/- theta, 180 +/- theta, 270 +/- theta, 360 +/- theta and -theta, whose functions reduce to functions of theta.
sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, with the related forms 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta and 1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta.
A function f with f(theta + p) = f(theta) for all theta, where the smallest such p is the period; 2*pi for sine and cosine, pi for tangent.
The set of angles for which a function is defined; e.g. tan theta is undefined where cos theta = 0.
The set of values a function can take; [-1, 1] for sine and cosine, all reals for tangent.
An even function satisfies f(-theta) = f(theta) (cosine, secant); an odd function satisfies f(-theta) = -f(theta) (sine, tangent, cotangent, cosecant).

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Trigonometric Functions-I (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for numerical problems. Use pi radians = 180 degrees, and take pi = 22/7 where a numerical value is needed unless stated otherwise.

questions.question: Convert (a) 150 degrees to radians and (b) 5*pi/6 radians to degrees.
questions.answer:
(a) Multiply by pi/180: 150 * pi/180 = 5*pi/6 radian.
(b) Multiply by 180/pi: (5*pi/6)(180/pi) = 5 * 30 = 150 degrees.
questions.explanation: Use pi radians = 180 degrees; deg->rad multiply by pi/180, rad->deg multiply by 180/pi.

questions.question: An arc of a circle of radius 14 cm subtends an angle of pi/3 radian at the centre. Find the length of the arc.
questions.answer:
Arc length s = r*theta with theta in radians.
s = 14 * (pi/3) = 14*pi/3 cm.
Taking pi = 22/7, s = 14 * (22/7) / 3 = (44)/3 = about 14.67 cm.
questions.explanation: Apply s = r*theta directly with theta in radians.

questions.question: State the ASTC rule and use it to give the sign of cos 200 degrees and of tan 300 degrees.
questions.answer:
ASTC: in quadrant I all functions are positive, in II only sine (and cosec), in III only tangent (and cot), in IV only cosine (and sec).
200 degrees lies in quadrant III, where cosine is negative, so cos 200 degrees is negative.
300 degrees lies in quadrant IV, where tangent is negative, so tan 300 degrees is negative.
questions.explanation: Identify the quadrant, then read off the sign from ASTC.

questions.question: Evaluate sin 30 * cos 60 + cos 30 * sin 60 using the standard-angle values.
questions.explanation: Substitute standard values; the result equals sin 90.

questions.question: If cos theta = -5/13 and theta lies in the third quadrant, find sin theta and tan theta.
questions.answer:
sin^2 theta = 1 - cos^2 theta = 1 - 25/169 = 144/169, so sin theta = +/- 12/13.
In the third quadrant sine is negative, so sin theta = -12/13.
tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = (-12/13)/(-5/13) = 12/5.
questions.explanation: Use sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 and fix signs by the quadrant.

questions.question: Prove the identity (1 + tan^2 theta) cos^2 theta = 1.
questions.answer:
Left side = (1 + tan^2 theta) cos^2 theta.
Since 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta = 1/cos^2 theta,
Left side = (1/cos^2 theta) * cos^2 theta = 1 = Right side.
Hence proved.

questions.question: State the period and range of the sine function and of the tangent function.
questions.answer:
Sine: period 2*pi (or 360 degrees); range [-1, 1].
Tangent: period pi (or 180 degrees); range all real numbers.
questions.explanation: Recall the standard periodicity and range facts.

questions.question: Show that sin(-theta) = -sin theta and cos(-theta) = cos theta, and hence evaluate sin(-45 degrees) and cos(-45 degrees).
questions.answer:
Replacing theta by -theta reflects P(x, y) on the terminal side to P'(x, -y): x is unchanged, y changes sign, r unchanged.
So sin(-theta) = (-y)/r = -sin theta, and cos(-theta) = x/r = cos theta.
Thus sin(-45 degrees) = -sin 45 = -1/sqrt2, and cos(-45 degrees) = cos 45 = 1/sqrt2.
questions.explanation: Use the reflection y -> -y; sine is odd, cosine is even.

questions.question: A circular wire of radius 21 cm is bent into an arc that subtends an angle of 60 degrees at the centre of a circle of radius 42 cm? Instead, solve: An arc of a circle of radius 42 cm has length 22 cm. Find the angle it subtends at the centre in radians and in degrees, and find the area of the corresponding sector.
questions.explanation: theta = s/r, convert to degrees with 180/pi, sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta.

questions.question: Using allied-angle relations, evaluate (a) sin 120 degrees, (b) cos 135 degrees, (c) tan 210 degrees and (d) cos 330 degrees. Show the reduction for each.
questions.answer:
(a) sin 120 = sin(180 - 60) = sin 60 = sqrt3/2 (quadrant II, sine positive).
(b) cos 135 = cos(180 - 45) = -cos 45 = -1/sqrt2 (quadrant II, cosine negative).
(c) tan 210 = tan(180 + 30) = tan 30 = 1/sqrt3 (quadrant III, tangent positive).
(d) cos 330 = cos(360 - 30) = cos 30 = sqrt3/2 (quadrant IV, cosine positive).
questions.explanation: Write each as 180/360 +/- (standard angle); name stays, sign from ASTC.

questions.question: Cosine is an even function while sine is an odd function.
pi radians = ______ degrees.
90 degrees in radian measure is ______.
To convert radians to degrees, multiply by ______.
The arc length of a circle is given by s = ______ (theta in radians).
An arc of radius 7 cm subtending 2 radians has length ______ cm.
The area of a sector of radius r and angle theta (radians) is ______.
With P(x, y) and r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), cos theta = ______.
The reciprocal of cos theta is ______.
By ASTC, in the third quadrant the positive functions are tangent and ______.
questions.explanation: Quadrant III: tan and cot positive.

questions.question: sin(90 + theta) = ______.
questions.explanation: Name changes, quadrant II sine positive.

questions.question: sin 60 degrees = ______.
tan 30 degrees = ______.
sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = ______.
The period of the cosine function is ______.
Since sine is odd, sin(-30 degrees) = ______.
Convert 75 degrees into radian measure.
Convert 4*pi/9 radian into degree measure.
Explain the difference between a positive and a negative angle.
questions.answer: An angle generated by anticlockwise rotation of the terminal side from the initial side is taken as positive; an angle generated by clockwise rotation is taken as negative. The sense of rotation, not just the size, fixes the sign.
questions.explanation: Sense of rotation determines the sign.

questions.question: Find the length of an arc of a circle of radius 9 cm that subtends an angle of 2/3 radian at the centre.
A pendulum 75 cm long swings through an angle of 0.4 radian. Find the length of the arc through which the tip moves.
questions.answer:
The tip moves along an arc of radius r = 75 cm through theta = 0.4 radian.
s = r*theta = 75 * 0.4 = 30 cm.
questions.explanation: Arc length formula with the pendulum length as radius.

questions.question: An arc of length 11 cm subtends an angle of pi/4 radian at the centre. Find the radius (take pi = 22/7).
Write the definitions of the six trigonometric functions using a point P(x, y) on the terminal side.
questions.answer: With r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2): sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x, cosec theta = r/y, sec theta = r/x, cot theta = x/y.

questions.question: The point P(-3, 4) lies on the terminal side of an angle theta. Find sin theta, cos theta and tan theta.
questions.answer:
r = sqrt((-3)^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9+16) = 5.
sin theta = y/r = 4/5.
cos theta = x/r = -3/5.
tan theta = y/x = 4/(-3) = -4/3.
questions.explanation: Compute r, then the ratios; note the signs.

questions.question: For what values of theta between 0 and 360 degrees is tan theta undefined, and why?
questions.answer: tan theta = y/x is undefined when x = 0, i.e. at theta = 90 degrees and theta = 270 degrees, because division by zero is not allowed (cos theta = 0 there).

questions.question: Using ASTC, state the sign of (a) cos 250 degrees and (b) sin 310 degrees.
questions.answer:
(a) 250 degrees is in quadrant III where cosine is negative, so cos 250 degrees is negative.
(b) 310 degrees is in quadrant IV where sine is negative, so sin 310 degrees is negative.
questions.explanation: Locate the quadrant and read ASTC.

questions.question: Reduce and evaluate cos(180 + 60 degrees) using allied-angle rules.
questions.answer:
180 + theta lies in quadrant III; the name stays as cosine and in quadrant III cosine is negative.
cos(180 + 60) = -cos 60 = -1/2.
questions.explanation: Even multiple of 90: name stays; sign from ASTC.

questions.question: Show that sin(90 + theta) = cos theta and cos(90 + theta) = -sin theta.
questions.answer:
90 + theta lies in quadrant II. It is an odd multiple of 90 degrees, so each name changes to its co-function.
In quadrant II sine is positive: sin(90 + theta) = +cos theta.
In quadrant II cosine is negative: cos(90 + theta) = -sin theta.
questions.explanation: Odd multiple: name changes; sign from quadrant II.

questions.question: Write the values of sin, cos and tan for 45 degrees.
Evaluate cos 30 cos 60 - sin 30 sin 60.
Using allied angles, evaluate sin 225 degrees and tan 240 degrees.
questions.answer:
sin 225 = sin(180 + 45) = -sin 45 = -1/sqrt2 (quadrant III, sine negative).
tan 240 = tan(180 + 60) = tan 60 = sqrt3 (quadrant III, tangent positive).
questions.explanation: Write as 180 + standard angle; sign from ASTC.

questions.question: State the three Pythagorean identities.
If tan theta = 4/3 and theta is acute, find sin theta and cos theta.
questions.answer:
For acute theta take a right triangle with opposite 4, adjacent 3, hypotenuse 5.
sin theta = 4/5 and cos theta = 3/5.
(Check: sin^2 + cos^2 = 16/25 + 9/25 = 1.)
questions.explanation: Use a 3-4-5 triangle or the identities.

questions.question: Prove that (sec theta - cos theta)(cosec theta - sin theta) = sin theta cos theta.
questions.answer:
sec theta - cos theta = 1/cos - cos = (1 - cos^2)/cos = sin^2/cos.
cosec theta - sin theta = 1/sin - sin = (1 - sin^2)/sin = cos^2/sin.
Product = (sin^2/cos)(cos^2/sin) = sin cos = sin theta cos theta. Proved.
questions.explanation: Combine to single fractions using the Pythagorean identity.

questions.question: State the domain and range of the cosine function.
questions.answer: Domain: all real numbers (every angle). Range: [-1, 1].
questions.explanation: cos is defined everywhere, values in [-1, 1].

questions.question: Describe in words the graph of y = sin theta over one period from 0 to 360 degrees.
questions.answer: Starting at 0 (sin 0 = 0) the curve rises to a maximum of +1 at 90 degrees, returns to 0 at 180 degrees, falls to a minimum of -1 at 270 degrees, and comes back to 0 at 360 degrees. It is a smooth wave oscillating between -1 and +1 and then repeats with period 2*pi.
questions.explanation: Zeros at 0, 180, 360; max at 90; min at 270.

questions.question: Evaluate cos(-150 degrees) using the even property of cosine.
questions.answer: cos is even, so cos(-150) = cos 150 = cos(180 - 30) = -cos 30 = -sqrt3/2.
questions.explanation: Use cos(-x)=cos x, then allied angle.

questions.question: Explain why sine is called an odd function and cosine an even function, referring to their graphs.
questions.answer: Replacing theta by -theta reflects P(x, y) to (x, -y): y changes sign, x does not. So sin(-theta) = -sin theta (odd) and cos(-theta) = cos theta (even). On the graph, the sine curve has point symmetry about the origin (odd), while the cosine curve is symmetric about the y-axis (even).

questions.question: Define radian measure and derive the relation pi radians = 180 degrees. Hence convert 135 degrees and 5*pi/4 radian, showing both conversions.
questions.answer:
A radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius. The full circumference 2*pi*r subtends the total angle 2*pi radians, and a full revolution is also 360 degrees, so 2*pi radians = 360 degrees, giving pi radians = 180 degrees.
Convert 135 degrees to radians: 135 * pi/180 = 3*pi/4 radian.
Convert 5*pi/4 radian to degrees: (5*pi/4)(180/pi) = 5 * 45 = 225 degrees.
questions.explanation: Definition, derivation, then the two conversions.

questions.question: A circle has radius 28 cm. An arc subtends an angle of 45 degrees at the centre. Find (a) the arc length and (b) the area of the sector. Take pi = 22/7.
questions.answer:
First convert the angle to radians: theta = 45 * pi/180 = pi/4 radian.
(a) Arc length s = r*theta = 28 * (pi/4) = 7*pi. With pi = 22/7, s = 7 * 22/7 = 22 cm.
(b) Sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta = (1/2)(28^2)(pi/4) = (1/2)(784)(pi/4) = 98*pi. With pi = 22/7, area = 98 * 22/7 = 14 * 22 = 308 cm^2.
questions.explanation: Convert to radians, then apply s = r*theta and (1/2) r^2 theta.

questions.question: Explain how the trigonometric functions of any angle are defined using coordinates, and use the definition to find all six functions of the angle whose terminal side passes through P(1, -sqrt3).
questions.answer:
Place the vertex at the origin with the initial side on the positive x-axis. Let P(x, y) lie on the terminal side at distance r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) > 0. Then sin = y/r, cos = x/r, tan = y/x, cosec = r/y, sec = r/x, cot = x/y.
For P(1, -sqrt3): r = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2.
sin theta = -sqrt3/2, cos theta = 1/2, tan theta = -sqrt3,
cosec theta = -2/sqrt3, sec theta = 2, cot theta = -1/sqrt3.
questions.explanation: State the coordinate definition, compute r, then all six ratios.

questions.question: Using allied-angle relations, evaluate each of sin 300 degrees, cos 225 degrees, tan 330 degrees and cot 135 degrees, stating the quadrant and sign in each case.
questions.answer:
sin 300 = sin(360 - 60) = -sin 60 = -sqrt3/2 (quadrant IV, sine negative).
cos 225 = cos(180 + 45) = -cos 45 = -1/sqrt2 (quadrant III, cosine negative).
tan 330 = tan(360 - 30) = -tan 30 = -1/sqrt3 (quadrant IV, tangent negative).
cot 135 = cot(180 - 45) = -cot 45 = -1 (quadrant II, cotangent negative).
questions.explanation: Write each as a multiple of 90/180/360 plus a standard angle; name stays for even multiples, sign from ASTC.

questions.question: Prepare the table of sin and cos for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, describe the pattern used to remember it, and hence write tan for each of these angles.
questions.answer:
sin: 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1 for 0, 30, 45, 60, 90.
cos: 1, sqrt3/2, 1/sqrt2, 1/2, 0 (the same list reversed).
Pattern: write 0,1,2,3,4 under the angles, divide by 4 and take the square root to get sin; read backwards for cos.
tan = sin/cos: tan 0 = 0, tan 30 = 1/sqrt3, tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt3, tan 90 is undefined (cos 90 = 0).
questions.explanation: Table, the sqrt((0..4)/4) pattern, then tan = sin/cos.

questions.question: Prove the identity (1 + cos theta)/(sin theta) + (sin theta)/(1 + cos theta) = 2 cosec theta.
questions.answer:
Take the left side over a common denominator sin theta (1 + cos theta):
Numerator = (1 + cos theta)^2 + sin^2 theta
= 1 + 2 cos theta + cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta
= 1 + 2 cos theta + 1   (since sin^2 + cos^2 = 1)
= 2 + 2 cos theta = 2(1 + cos theta).
So LHS = 2(1 + cos theta) / [sin theta (1 + cos theta)] = 2/sin theta = 2 cosec theta = RHS. Proved.
questions.explanation: Common denominator, expand, use sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, cancel.

questions.question: Compare the graphs of y = sin theta and y = cos theta over 0 to 360 degrees, and state the domain, range and period of each.
questions.answer: Both are smooth waves oscillating between -1 and +1 with period 2*pi (360 degrees) and domain all real numbers. y = sin theta starts at 0, peaks +1 at 90 degrees, is 0 at 180 degrees, dips to -1 at 270 degrees and back to 0 at 360 degrees. y = cos theta starts at its maximum +1 at 0, is 0 at 90 degrees, -1 at 180 degrees, 0 at 270 degrees and +1 at 360 degrees. The cosine curve is the sine curve shifted 90 degrees to the left, since cos theta = sin(theta + 90 degrees). For both, domain = all reals and range = [-1, 1].
questions.explanation: Describe both waves, the 90-degree shift, and give domain/range/period.

questions.question: State the negative-angle formulas for the six trigonometric functions, explain them from the coordinate definition, and evaluate sin(-120 degrees), cos(-120 degrees) and tan(-120 degrees).
questions.answer:
Replacing theta by -theta sends P(x, y) to (x, -y): sin(-theta) = -sin theta, cos(-theta) = cos theta, tan(-theta) = -tan theta, cosec(-theta) = -cosec theta, sec(-theta) = sec theta, cot(-theta) = -cot theta.
Now: sin(-120) = -sin 120 = -sin(180-60) = -sqrt3/2.
cos(-120) = cos 120 = cos(180-60) = -cos 60 = -1/2.
tan(-120) = -tan 120 = -tan(180-60) = -(-tan 60) = tan 60 = sqrt3.
questions.explanation: Reflection y -> -y gives odd/even behaviour; then evaluate with allied angles.

questions.question: A big Ferris wheel makes one full turn as its cabins rotate about the centre. Engineers describe cabin positions using angles in both degrees and radians. (a) Through how many radians does a cabin move in one complete revolution? (b) Convert 120 degrees to radians. (c) Convert 3*pi/2 radian to degrees. (d) If a cabin has turned 90 degrees from the start, what is this in radians?
questions.answer:
(a) One revolution = 2*pi radians.
(b) 120 * pi/180 = 2*pi/3 radian.
(c) (3*pi/2)(180/pi) = 270 degrees.
(d) 90 * pi/180 = pi/2 radian.
questions.explanation: Uses 1 rev = 2*pi and the pi/180 and 180/pi conversion factors.

questions.question: A circular running track has radius 50 m. A runner covers part of the track along an arc. (a) State the arc-length formula. (b) If the runner sweeps an angle of 1.2 radian at the centre, find the arc length. (c) What angle (in radians) corresponds to an arc of 40 m? (d) Find the area of the sector swept in part (b).
questions.answer:
(a) s = r*theta with theta in radians.
(b) s = 50 * 1.2 = 60 m.
(c) theta = s/r = 40/50 = 0.8 radian.
(d) Area = (1/2) r^2 theta = (1/2)(2500)(1.2) = 1500 m^2.
questions.explanation: Direct use of s = r*theta and (1/2) r^2 theta.

questions.question: On a coordinate grid, the terminal side of an angle theta passes through the point P(-8, 6). (a) Find r. (b) Find sin theta. (c) Find cos theta. (d) Find tan theta.
questions.explanation: Compute r, then each ratio, keeping track of signs (quadrant II).

questions.question: A student must decide the sign of trigonometric functions in different quadrants using ASTC. (a) State what ASTC stands for. (b) In which quadrant are only tangent and cotangent positive? (c) What is the sign of sin 200 degrees? (d) What is the sign of cos 100 degrees?
questions.answer:
(a) ASTC: All (I), Sine (II), Tangent (III), Cosine (IV) are positive respectively.
(b) The third quadrant (180 to 270 degrees).
(c) 200 degrees is in quadrant III, so sin 200 degrees is negative.
(d) 100 degrees is in quadrant II, so cos 100 degrees is negative.
questions.explanation: Apply the ASTC rule quadrant by quadrant.

questions.question: A surveyor uses standard-angle values while measuring inclinations. (a) Write the value of tan 60 degrees. (b) Evaluate sin 30 + cos 60. (c) Evaluate 2 sin 45 cos 45. (d) Evaluate tan 45 - sin 90.

A physics problem gives sin theta = 5/13 with theta in the first quadrant. (a) Which identity relates sin and cos? (b) Find cos theta. (c) Find tan theta. (d) Verify that 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta for this theta.
questions.answer:
(a) sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1.
(b) cos^2 = 1 - 25/169 = 144/169, so cos theta = 12/13 (first quadrant, positive).
(c) tan theta = sin/cos = (5/13)/(12/13) = 5/12.
(d) 1 + tan^2 = 1 + 25/144 = 169/144. sec^2 = 1/cos^2 = 169/144. They are equal, verifying the identity.
questions.explanation: Pythagorean identity to get cos and tan, then check 1+tan^2=sec^2.

questions.question: A teacher asks students to simplify trigonometric expressions using identities. (a) Simplify sin theta cosec theta. (b) Simplify (1 - sin^2 theta). (c) Simplify tan theta cot theta. (d) Simplify sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta.
questions.answer:
(a) sin theta cosec theta = sin theta (1/sin theta) = 1.
(b) 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta.
(c) tan theta cot theta = tan theta (1/tan theta) = 1.
(d) sec^2 theta - tan^2 theta = 1 (from 1 + tan^2 = sec^2).
questions.explanation: Uses reciprocal relations and the Pythagorean identity.

questions.question: A signal is modelled by a sine wave. Students study the properties of y = sin theta. (a) What is its period? (b) What is its range? (c) At what angle between 0 and 360 degrees is the graph a maximum? (d) At what angle is it a minimum?
questions.answer:
(a) Period = 2*pi (360 degrees).
(b) Range = [-1, 1].
(c) Maximum +1 at theta = 90 degrees.
(d) Minimum -1 at theta = 270 degrees.
questions.explanation: Recall the shape and key points of the sine wave.

questions.question: A student compares the domains and ranges of the six functions. (a) For which functions is the range [-1, 1]? (b) For which functions is the range all real numbers? (c) Where is tan theta undefined between 0 and 360 degrees? (d) What is the period of tan theta?
questions.answer:
(a) sine and cosine have range [-1, 1].
(b) tangent and cotangent have range all real numbers.
(c) tan theta is undefined at 90 degrees and 270 degrees (where cos theta = 0).
(d) The period of tan theta is pi (180 degrees).
questions.explanation: Domain, range and period facts for the six functions.

questions.question: An engineer uses the fact that trigonometric functions of negative angles relate to those of positive angles. (a) State whether sine is odd or even. (b) State whether cosine is odd or even. (c) Evaluate sin(-90 degrees). (d) Evaluate cos(-60 degrees).
questions.answer:
(a) Sine is an odd function: sin(-theta) = -sin theta.
(b) Cosine is an even function: cos(-theta) = cos theta.
(c) sin(-90) = -sin 90 = -1.
(d) cos(-60) = cos 60 = 1/2.
questions.explanation: Apply odd/even properties to evaluate negative-angle values.
